practice1.hint: The pipeline is only finished when the data survives leaving the program. Formatting it into a string and printing it proves the first half; reading it back proves the rest.

questions.prompt: In the weather collector, why is the API call wrapped in try/except?
choices: Because a network call can fail for reasons your code cannot prevent
questions.explain: A timeout, a dropped connection or a 500 are all outside your control. A collector meant to run unattended has to survive them rather than stop.

questions.prompt: Which does raise_for_status() save you from writing?
choices: The if that checks response.status_code yourself
questions.explain: It turns a bad status into an exception, so the failure joins the except block you already have instead of needing a branch of its own.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the data collection pipeline in order.
items: Request the data from the API
Parse the JSON reply into Python objects
Add a timestamp to the record
Write the record to a file
questions.explain: Each step consumes what the one before it produced. That is also the order to build it in, testing each part before adding the next.

questions.prompt: Which Unit 9 pieces does the weather collector combine?
choices: An HTTP request to an API
questions.explain: Fetch, parse, stamp, save. There is nothing recursive in it, and reaching for recursion because the unit taught it would be the wrong instinct.

questions.prompt: Before building, break the project into ___ that can each be tested on their own.
questions.explain: A pipeline built in one go fails as one thing, and you cannot tell which link broke. Testable parts are what makes the failure findable.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Walk the data from the server to the disk and name each step, including what you do when a step fails.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Name the project and then the two or three Unit 9 pieces it would need. Being specific about the pieces is what makes it a plan.
